page.title: Flavor Ingredient Finder | Simon Cui
hero.title: Flavor ingredient finder
hero.intro: Flavorists choose from thousands of ingredient molecules: for a client brief they look for ingredients with the target flavor, and when an ingredient is restricted or unavailable they look for one that smells similar. This tool does both with AI-predicted odor profiles: search ingredients by target flavor, or find substitutes for a molecule. The results are a shortlist; a flavorist's judgment and sensory testing still decide.

results.title: How well does it work?
results.intro: Both modes are evaluated on the scaffold-split test set of odor-predictor (488 molecules), computed once at the end; the odor-similarity method was chosen beforehand on the validation set only.
results.a_title: Find by brief: do the top-ranked molecules really have the descriptor?
results.a_text: For each descriptor, test molecules are ranked by predicted probability; precision@10 / @50 is the share of the top 10 / 50 that are labelled with that descriptor, averaged over 138 descriptors.
results.a_take: The model's top molecules are far better than random, but about the same as a simple fingerprint + logistic regression, with no advantage. A likely reason: ranking for one descriptor depends mostly on a few typical substructures (lactone rings, sulfur atoms), which fingerprints also capture.
results.b_title: Find substitutes: do the most similar molecules really smell alike?
results.b_text: For each test molecule, the 10 most similar molecules are found and the mean overlap of their true odor labels with the query's is computed (Jaccard, 0 to 1, higher = more alike). Three ways are compared: by predicted odor profile (this page's "odor similarity"), by structure (Tanimoto), and at random.
results.b_take: Molecules found by predicted odor profile share clearly more odor labels with the query than those found by structure (95% CI of the difference {lo} to {hi}), and are better for {share}% of queries. The mean overlap is only about {mean}, so treat the results as a shortlist. The gain is larger for acyclic molecules, but these were split one by one at random, so homologues can sit in both training and test sets and this part may be optimistic.
limits.title: Limitations
limits.1: Based on predicted odor categories; says nothing about odor intensity, thresholds or actual sensory performance.
limits.2: Stability, solubility, cost and availability are not considered.
limits.3: Safety and regulatory compliance of any substitute must be checked separately.
limits.4: Results are a shortlist that needs a flavorist's judgment and sensory testing.
footer.data: Data and acknowledgements: the odor model was trained on data from The Good Scents Company and Leffingwell & Associates (Sanchez-Lengeling et al., 2019, arXiv:1910.10685, CC BY-NC), curated and merged by OpenPOM (Barsainyan et al., 2023); the raw odor labels are not redistributed here and the page shows model predictions only. The model and its predictions are for non-commercial academic demonstration only.

b.intro: Pick a molecule: the page finds the 20 molecules with the most similar predicted odor profile and also shows how similar their structures are. Molecules that smell alike but differ in structure (orange) are the most valuable substitutes, as they may avoid the original's regulatory, patent or supply issues.
bg.diacetyl: Diacetyl itself is a permitted food flavoring. The concern is occupational inhalation in production settings: workers in flavoring and microwave popcorn production who breathed diacetyl vapor over time have developed a serious lung disease (bronchiolitis obliterans). It is not a food-safety issue. In 2016 the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) recommended exposure limits of 5 ppb as an 8-hour time-weighted average and 25 ppb for 15 minutes; these are recommendations, not enforceable OSHA standards. Hence the real industry need for substitutes.
src.diacetyl: Sources: NIOSH (2016). Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Diacetyl and 2,3-Pentanedione. DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2016-111; OSHA, Flavorings-Related Lung Disease.
bg.coumarin: EU: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 on flavourings, Annex III Part A: coumarin (1,2-benzopyrone) shall not be added as such to food; Part B: in compound foods to which flavourings or food ingredients with flavouring properties (such as cinnamon) have been added, coumarin naturally present may not exceed 50 mg/kg in traditional and/or seasonal bakery ware with a reference to cinnamon in the labelling, 20 mg/kg in breakfast cereals including muesli, 15 mg/kg in other fine bakery ware and 5 mg/kg in desserts; the limits do not apply when only fresh, dried or frozen herbs and spices, and no flavourings, have been added. US: under 21 CFR 189.130, food containing added coumarin, as such or as a constituent of tonka beans or tonka extract, is deemed adulterated.
src.coumarin: Sources: Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008, Official Journal of the European Union L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 34, Annex III; 21 CFR 189.130. Regulatory information is for reference only; the latest official texts prevail.
bg.vanillin: Natural vanillin comes from vanilla pods and the yield is low: about 500 kg of pods give 1 kg of vanillin, a slow, laborious and costly process. Less than 1% of the world's vanillin comes from the vanilla orchid; the rest is mostly made by chemical synthesis or from lignin.
src.vanillin: Source: Gallage NJ, et al. Vanillin formation from ferulic acid in Vanilla planifolia is catalysed by a single enzyme. Nature Communications 2014, 5:4037. doi:10.1038/ncomms5037.
